clue.text: Beastly downpour?

parts.note: a heavy shower of rain pictured as animals falling from the sky, the 'beastly' being literal

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles about a nasty, heavy shower of rain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beastly' reads as 'horrible', but here it means 'made of beasts': the idiom for very heavy rain names two household pets.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes torrential rain, as in saying it is pouring hard outside.

clue.text: Didn't go much on Arthur's place!

parts.note: the opposite of going is coming, so 'didn't go' gives came
a lot means much

explanation.surface: Someone was unimpressed by King Arthur's home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Didn't go much on' is a British idiom for disliking something, so the surface reads as a put-down of Arthur's home.
explanation.definitionFit: In legend the court and castle of King Arthur stood at this fabled site.

clue.text: Go to bed, having lost direction in Italy

indicators.note: having lost says a letter is dropped from the phrase for going to bed

parts.note: to turn in is to go to bed
N, north, is a compass direction

explanation.surface: A traveller in Italy got lost and decided to go to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having lost' removes N from TURN IN.
explanation.definitionFit: The city is in the north-west of Italy, capital of Piedmont.

clue.text: Doctor meant to go round some accommodation

indicators.note: to go round says the rearranged letters surround the word for some
to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters of meant are rearranged

parts.note: a part is some of something

explanation.surface: A GP intends to visit some lodgings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' rearranges MEANT into AMENT, and 'to go round' has those letters surround the piece meaning some, after the first A.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat is a set of rooms used as living quarters.

clue.text: Bother! Make a run for it!

explanation.surface: Someone curses, then flees.
explanation.definitionFit: Both an exclamation of mild annoyance, like 'Drat!', and a verb for sprinting off in a hurry.

clue.text: Deck in a thousand-tonner at sea

indicators.note: at sea means confused or adrift, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: Something sits on the deck of a huge thousand-ton ship out at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at sea' rearranges A, M and TONNER. 'Deck' is a verb, not part of a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: To deck is to adorn or decorate.

clue.text: Shots of Surrey opener stir the oval

indicators.note: the opener of a word is its first letter
to stir is to mix up, so the letters of oval are rearranged

explanation.surface: Surrey's opening batsman plays shots that set the Oval buzzing.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oval is Surrey's cricket ground in London, and an opener is a batsman; here 'opener' takes S and 'stir' makes ALVO from OVAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A salvo is a simultaneous burst of gunfire.

clue.text: Left in a state of wretchedness, or very near

indicators.note: in says the letter for left is placed inside the word for wretchedness

parts.note: misery is a state of wretchedness

explanation.surface: Someone abandoned in misery, or close to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'very near' means mean or stingy, not close by.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Near' is an old colloquial word for tight-fisted, so very near is stingy.

clue.text: One abandoned by actors on tour

parts.note: the cast is the actors in a production
a touring company is away from home

explanation.surface: A performer is left behind by the rest of the company on tour.
explanation.definitionFit: A castaway is someone shipwrecked or marooned and left alone.

clue.text: People in serious offence

parts.note: mortals are human beings, people

explanation.surface: Some people are involved in a grave crime.
explanation.definitionFit: In Catholic teaching this grave sin cuts the soul off from grace.

clue.text: Starring roles for ushers

explanation.surface: Ushers getting the main parts in a show.
explanation.definitionFit: Principal parts in a play are the leads, and to usher someone is to guide or lead them.

clue.text: A good one is important to one bowling from end to end

definitions.text: A good one is important to one bowling

explanation.surface: Advice for a cricket bowler, and a measure of distance.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the bowler delivers the ball to the batsman; where it bounces is its 'length', and a good one is hard to hit.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a bowler aims for a good length, where the ball pitches; the word also means the measurement of something end to end.

clue.text: Phoney claim of poverty took in a holy man

indicators.note: took in says the claim surrounds the abbreviation for a holy man

parts.note: 'I'm poor' is what one says to claim poverty
ST, saint, is a holy man

explanation.surface: A fraud pleading poverty fooled a saintly man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Phoney' is a noun here: a fake person.
explanation.definitionFit: A pretender who deceives others by posing as someone else is a fake, a fraud.

clue.text: Moderate one's anger

explanation.surface: Advice to calm down one's rage.
explanation.definitionFit: To temper is to tone down or soften, and a temper is a fit of rage.

clue.text: Male showing off raincoat to his doctor

parts.note: a mac, short for mackintosh, is a raincoat
MO is a medical officer, a doctor

explanation.surface: A man shows his raincoat to his doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: Exaggerated masculine pride and bravado is this kind of swaggering display.

clue.text: Blocking — the road?

parts.note: something that obstructs is standing on the road or path, 'way' being a road

explanation.surface: Something is blocking the road.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for obstructing is read literally: a 'way' is a road, so to be on it is to block it.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means obstructing or being a nuisance, literally standing on the path.

clue.text: The most popular songs about apartheid

indicators.note: about signals that the letters of apartheid are turned around and rearranged

explanation.surface: Chart-topping protest songs against South African segregation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'concerning'; it rearranges APARTHEID.
explanation.definitionFit: This was the weekly chart ranking the best-selling records.

clue.text: Starts the game, giving thrills to cricket side

parts.note: kicks are thrills, as in doing something for kicks
the off side is one half of a cricket field

explanation.surface: A match begins, delighting a cricket team.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the field is split into the off side and the leg side, either side of the batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: In football a match begins with the first kick of the ball from the centre spot.

clue.text: Clock at one perhaps — have a drink

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters could be arranged otherwise

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Seeing one o'clock on the clock, someone decides to have a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges CLOCK, AT and I.
explanation.definitionFit: A mixed alcoholic beverage such as a martini or margarita.

clue.text: Fall of rotter in law-suit

indicators.note: in places the word for rotter inside the word for lawsuit

parts.note: a case is a lawsuit brought before a court
a cad is a rotter, a dishonourable man

explanation.surface: The downfall of a scoundrel in court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fall' is a waterfall, not a downfall.
explanation.definitionFit: A cascade is a waterfall, a series of small falls of water.

clue.text: Stopped wearing corsets

explanation.surface: Someone stopped putting on corsets.
explanation.definitionFit: To stay is to halt or remain, and stays are the stiffening strips of a corset, so a stayed figure is laced into one.

clue.text: Do have a flutter, old lady!

parts.note: to have a flutter is British slang for placing a small bet

explanation.surface: Encouraging an elderly woman to place a bet.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'flutter' is a small bet in British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A dowager is a widow holding a title from her late husband, typically elderly.

clue.text: Larks in a strange land

indicators.note: strange signals the letters are put in an odd new arrangement

explanation.surface: Songbirds found in an unfamiliar country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange land' reads as one phrase for a foreign country, but 'strange' is the anagram signal working on the birds and the word before A, and 'land' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The island nation south of India, formerly Ceylon, is a country.

clue.text: A fateful day for military assistants

parts.note: the Ides of March was the day Julius Caesar was assassinated

explanation.surface: An ominous day for soldiers' helpers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ides were the middle of a Roman month; the Ides of March was famously fatal for Caesar.
explanation.definitionFit: Aides-de-camp are officers who assist senior commanders.

clue.text: Capital maxim in time of conflict

parts.note: war is a time of conflict
a saw is a wise saying, a maxim

explanation.surface: A capital saying in wartime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' looks like 'excellent', but it means a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: The city is the capital of Poland.

clue.text: Criticism for staff

explanation.surface: Criticism directed at employees.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone stick is to criticise them harshly, and a stick is a walking staff.

clue.text: Some passer-by from Belgrade?

indicators.note: some says only part of the word passer-by is taken

explanation.surface: A pedestrian from the Serbian capital.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by example: a person from Belgrade, Serbia's capital.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Serbia, whose capital is Belgrade, is one of its nationals.

clue.text: Directed me to help out

indicators.note: out says the word for help lies outside, with me inside it

parts.note: aid is help

explanation.surface: Someone told me to lend a hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'help out' reads as 'assist'; here 'out' puts AID outside ME.
explanation.definitionFit: To aim something is to point or direct it at a target.

clue.text: Carrying on business — with a knife?

explanation.surface: A shady trade conducted with a blade.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm that is running is functioning, and a surgeon cutting a patient is in surgery.

clue.text: Criminal gives Peter a wave

parts.note: peter is old underworld slang for a safe
a breaker is a large wave breaking on the shore

explanation.surface: A crook waves to a man called Peter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peter' looks like a name; in thieves' slang a peter is a safe.
explanation.definitionFit: A thief who cracks open strongboxes is a burglar of a specialised kind.
